# Overview

blotIt aligns biological replicate data, e.g. quantitative western blots or qPCR, on a common scale. It is a rewrite of [blotIt2](https://github.com/dkaschek/blotIt2) by Daniel Kaschek.

## Installation

```r
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("JetiLab/blotIt")
```

The analytic model inversion uses the Python package SymPy through reticulate, which is installed on first use. Without it, blotIt inverts the model numerically.

# Usage

## Data import

Measurements are usually stored in wide CSV files: some description columns followed by one column per target.

```r
library(blotIt)
exampleDataPath <- system.file("extdata", "simDataWide.csv", package = "blotIt")
importedData <- readWide(exampleDataPath, description = seq_len(3))
```

`description` gives the indices of the description columns (here `time`, `condition`, `experiment`). `readWide()` returns a long table with the description columns, `name` (the target) and `value`.

## Alignment

```r
out <- alignReplicates(
  data = importedData,
  model = "yi / sj",
  errorModel = "value * sigmaR",
  biological = yi ~ name + time + condition,
  scaling = sj ~ name + experiment,
  error = sigmaR ~ name
)
```

- `model`: the measured value as a function of the parameters. Here the true value `yi` divided by a scaling factor `sj`.
- `errorModel`: the standard deviation of a measurement. `value` stands for the model prediction, so `value * sigmaR` is a relative error.
- `biological`: the parameters on the left differ between levels of the columns on the right. Here `yi` has one value per target, time point and condition.
- `scaling`: as `biological`, for the scaling parameters. Here `sj` has one value per target and experiment.
- `error`: as `biological`, for the error parameters. `~ name` gives one value per target.

The result is a list. `aligned` has one row per biological level with the estimate on the common scale and its uncertainty. `scaled` has the measurements mapped to the common scale, `prediction` the model prediction on the original scale, and `parameter` the parameter table. See `?alignReplicates` for all entries.

## Plotting

```r
plotIt(out, plotPoints = "scaled", plotLine = "aligned")
```

`plotPoints` and `plotLine` name the tables drawn as points and as lines with error bands: `"original"`, `"scaled"`, `"prediction"` or `"aligned"`. Usual combinations:

- `plotPoints = "original", plotLine = "prediction"`: raw data with the fit.
- `plotPoints = "scaled", plotLine = "aligned"`: data on the common scale with the aligned course.
- `plotPoints = "aligned", plotLine = "aligned"`: the aligned course only.

Further arguments subset the data, e.g. `name == "pAKT"`.

## Start values and multistart

All parameters start at 1 by default. `parinit` sets start values on the scale of the parameter table, either one number per parameter or a vector named by level:

```r
out <- alignReplicates(
  data = importedData,
  model = "yi / sj",
  errorModel = "value * sigmaR",
  biological = yi ~ name + time + condition,
  scaling = sj ~ name + experiment,
  error = sigmaR ~ name,
  parinit = list(sigmaR = 0.1, sj = c(pAKT_1 = 2)),
  multistart = 20,
  multistartSd = 2,
  cores = 4
)
plotWaterfall(out)
```

With `multistart > 1`, starts 2 to `multistart` perturb the start values by normal noise with standard deviation `multistartSd` on the fit scale. `cores > 1` runs the starts in parallel processes (not on Windows); the result does not depend on `cores`. `plotWaterfall()` shows the sorted final objective values of all starts per target. A plateau at the lowest value that several starts reach indicates the global optimum.

## Error parameters with own levels

`error` accepts a list of formulas, one per error parameter group:

```r
alignReplicates(
  data = combinedData,
  model = "yi + sj",
  errorModel = "sqrt(exp(2 * sigmaA) + isWB * exp(2 * sigmaB))",
  biological = yi ~ name + time,
  scaling = sj ~ name + gel,
  error = list(sigmaA ~ name + modality, sigmaB ~ name + modality),
  fitLogscale = FALSE
)
```

Here `sigmaA` and `sigmaB` have one value per target and modality. Parameters without influence on the likelihood, such as `sigmaB` for levels where the covariate `isWB` is 0, are not fitted and reported as `NA`.

## Outliers

With `likelihood = "t"`, each data point follows a Student-t distribution with `df` degrees of freedom (default 5) and scale `errorModel`. Single outliers then shift the aligned values much less than with the normal likelihood.

```r
out <- alignReplicates(..., likelihood = "t", df = 5)
```

# Methods

## Likelihood

For each target, the data \(Y_k\) are modeled as \(Y_k \sim N(f(p_k), \sigma(p_k)^2)\), where \(f\) is `model`, \(\sigma\) is `errorModel`, and \(p_k\) holds the biological, scaling and error parameters of the levels of data point \(k\). The parameters maximize the likelihood. With `normalize = TRUE`, a penalty fixes the mean of the first biological parameter to 1. With `fitLogscale = TRUE`, the logarithms of the parameters are fitted. With `likelihood = "t"`, the normal density is replaced by a Student-t density with scale \(\sigma(p_k)\); the fit uses iteratively reweighted Gauss-Newton steps and the uncertainties the expected Fisher information.

Targets whose data split into blocks without shared scaling levels are fitted separately.

With `normalizeInput = TRUE`, each block is divided by its mean if all values are positive, and centered otherwise.

## Optimization

`trust()` is a trust-region method with the Gauss-Newton Hessian. If the eigendecomposition of the Hessian fails, it takes a steepest-descent step within the trust region and shrinks the region, instead of stopping.

Above `optControls$structuredThreshold` parameters (default 5000), a sparse Levenberg-Marquardt method replaces it. Each data point depends on one parameter per model symbol, so the Hessian is sparse with a diagonal biological block. Steps are solved by sparse Cholesky factorization with a Sherman-Morrison correction for the normalization penalty, at \(O(n)\) cost per iteration for \(n\) parameters.

## Uncertainties

Parameter uncertainties are the square roots of the diagonal of the inverse Fisher information, with a Bessel correction for the number of fitted parameters. On the sparse path, the diagonal of the inverse is computed from the Schur complement of the scaling and error block, without forming the dense inverse. The measurements are mapped to the common scale by solving \(f(p) = Y_k\) for the biological parameter, analytically with SymPy where possible and numerically with nleqslv otherwise. Their errors follow from Gaussian error propagation through this inverse.
